name: Security Governance and Risk Management
blurb: Who owns AI risk, how it reaches the register, the policies that decide which systems may act on untrusted content, and the accountability that survives an incident.

topics.body: Governance owns the decision that no filter can make: which systems are permitted to act on untrusted content at all, and with what authority. A risk register entry for an AI assistant that reads external content and holds write access is describing a standing injection exposure, and the accountable owner has to accept, constrain, or decline it explicitly. Mapping that decision to the NIST AI RMF and recording it beats discovering after an incident that nobody decided.
topics.name: Prompt Injection
topics.blurb: Direct and indirect prompt injection: how instructions hidden in content hijack model behavior, documented attacks, and current defenses.

topics.body: Model selection is a governance decision with a jailbreak dimension: labs publish system cards and safety evaluations that differ meaningfully, and an enterprise choosing a foundation model is choosing a jailbreak-resistance posture it never tested itself. Governance also owns acceptable-use policy for internal users, because the employee probing the corporate assistant with jailbreak prompts is generating exactly the evidence a regulator or plaintiff later asks about.
topics.name: Jailbreaks
topics.blurb: Techniques that bypass model safety training, and how labs measure and patch against them.

topics.body: Intelligence corruption belongs on the risk register as its own category, distinct from breach: the asset damaged is the model's judgment, and the loss event is bad decisions made at scale before anyone notices. NIST AI 100-2 gives governance a shared vocabulary for these attack classes, and a register that names poisoning explicitly forces the ownership and detection-investment conversations that generic cyber entries let slide.
topics.name: Model and Data Poisoning
topics.blurb: Corrupting training data or model weights to plant backdoors and biases, and the research on detecting it.

topics.body: Concentration is the governance-level supply chain risk: when many of your vendors quietly run on the same one or two foundation model providers, a single upstream incident, deprecation, or terms change propagates through products that look independent on the vendor map. A foundation-model concentration analysis, tracing which upstream models your portfolio actually depends on, is the AI equivalent of the critical-vendor analysis regulators already expect for cloud.
topics.name: AI Supply Chain Attacks
topics.blurb: Compromised models, datasets, and packages upstream: malicious model files, dependency attacks, opaque fourth-party model chains, AI bills of materials, and registry integrity.

topics.body: Governance sets the rule the tooling enforces: a written classification of what may enter prompts, what may enter fine-tunes, and what may never touch an external model, with the accountable owner named for each AI system that processes regulated data. Without that policy layer, every technical control is guessing at a standard nobody wrote down.
topics.name: Data Leakage
topics.blurb: Training data extraction, membership inference, and models revealing what they should not.

topics.body: For a frontier lab the weights are the crown jewels, and for any enterprise with a fine-tuned model they are a concentrated asset carrying training investment and embedded data. Governance treats weight custody as a named risk: where copies live, who can export them, and what contractual protections cover the providers holding them. Published security frameworks from the labs themselves, and independent analyses of weight-theft attack vectors, give the register real content, including the insider and infrastructure paths that matter more than exotic attacks.
topics.name: Model Theft
topics.blurb: Weight exfiltration and model extraction through APIs, and what providers disclose about protecting them.

topics.body: Shadow AI is the risk category the register never sees: business units adopting AI tools on corporate cards and browser extensions faster than procurement and security review can track, so the official inventory describes the enterprise as it was, not as it is. Prohibition fails because demand is real; the working answer is a sanctioning pathway that converts rogue adoption into governed capability, offering an approved route fast enough that going around it stops being worth it, and updating the inventory continuously rather than annually.
topics.name: Shadow AI
topics.blurb: Unsanctioned AI use inside organizations: the exposure it creates and how enterprises detect and govern it.

topics.body: Threat-intelligence tracking of this category needs discipline, because the hype outruns the evidence. Primary sources, lab threat reports, government advisories, and annual internet-crime statistics, document what AI-assisted attacks actually look like in practice, and governance should calibrate investment against that documented picture rather than against vendor marketing in either direction.
topics.name: AI-enabled Malware
topics.blurb: What is documented, by primary sources, about AI-assisted malicious code and the vendor and government reporting on it.

topics.body: The legal landscape is moving fast and unevenly: dozens of state bills address synthetic media across elections, intimate imagery, and fraud, the EU AI Act imposes labeling duties on AI-generated content, and disclosure obligations increasingly attach to enterprises deploying synthetic media in products or marketing. Governance tracks which duties apply where the enterprise operates, and this site's state-law tracker counts the live bill landscape on this page.
topics.name: Deepfakes and Synthetic Identity
topics.blurb: Synthetic media fraud, identity spoofing, detection methods, and the laws responding to them.

topics.body: Awareness programs built on spot-the-typo are obsolete, and policy has to carry more of the load: payment changes, credential resets, and data requests verified through independent channels regardless of how convincing the request sounds, with training updated to cover voice cloning and the documented executive-impersonation patterns from federal advisories. The policy that survives AI phishing is the one that never trusted message quality as a signal.
topics.name: AI Phishing and Social Engineering
topics.blurb: How generated text and voice change phishing at scale, per published incident and vendor reporting.

topics.body: Governance and risk tooling for AI answers the register's new questions: AI system inventory and discovery, posture management across model deployments, policy engines that map AI use against frameworks like the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act, and evidence automation that keeps compliance artifacts current at the pace AI systems actually change. The category test is whether the tool maintains a living picture, an inventory that updates itself, or just produces another binder that ages from the day it is exported.
topics.name: AI Security Tooling
topics.blurb: The defensive tooling landscape, organized by six security domains: Security Governance and Risk Management, Security Operations, Architecture and Engineering, Application and Product Security, Third-Party and Supply Chain Risk, and Data Protection and Privacy.

topics.body: Every agent identity needs a named accountable human owner, because delegated authority without an owner is the accountability vacuum in credential form: when an agent acts, the question of who decided must have an answer on file. Governance maintains the agent inventory with owners, granted authorities, and review dates, and treats an ownerless credential as an incident, not a housekeeping item.
topics.name: Agent and Non-Human Identity
topics.blurb: The explosion of machine identities: agent credentials, delegated authority, revocation, and the lateral movement paths nobody is watching.

topics.body: Autonomy is earned, not configured: governance defines the tiers of action an agent may take alone, with human review, or not at all, and expands an agent's tier only on evidence from adversarial evaluation and operating history. A supervision model that grants full autonomy on day one is not a policy, it is the absence of one recorded in writing.
topics.name: AI Agent Security
topics.blurb: Agent kill chains, cascading multi-agent failure, circuit breakers, agent-to-agent trust boundaries, and runtime supervision of autonomous systems.

topics.body: The decision rights question, which containment and response actions AI may execute without a human, is a governance decision that most SOCs are currently making implicitly through tool configuration. Making it explicit, recording it, and reviewing it as the AI's track record accumulates converts an unexamined default into a governed one, and gives the board a truthful answer about how much of security response is automated.
topics.name: AI in Security Operations
topics.blurb: Defending with AI: machine-speed investigation, human supervision models, automation bias, kill-switch protocols, and securing the SOC's own AI.

topics.body: Impact assessments are where AI privacy risk becomes visible before deployment, and regulator guidance now expects them for AI processing: lawful basis mapped for training and inference separately, automated decision-making obligations identified, and records of processing that describe model pipelines truthfully. Governance also owns the answer to consent theater, whether the notice actually describes what the system does with data, including what it derives.
topics.name: AI Privacy and Data Protection
topics.blurb: The deletion problem in trained models, inference as data collection, memory sprawl, purpose enforcement, and cross-border inference.

topics.body: Adversarial evaluation is where the evidence to expand autonomy comes from: an agent earns a wider action envelope by surviving structured attack campaigns, and governance can point to the test record when it grants the expansion. Disclosure practices, what gets reported to whom when red teams find systemic weaknesses, and the external evaluation ecosystem, including government AI security institutes, complete the accountability loop.
topics.name: AI Red Teaming and Adversarial Evaluation
topics.blurb: Continuous adversarial testing of AI systems: methods, benchmarks, disclosure practices, and the evidence that earns expanded autonomy.

topics.body: Governance owns the policy that says AI generated code meets the same bar as human code, and that AI features pass AI specific tests before release. It decides which assistants developers may use, what code and data those tools may see, and how SSDF conformance is evidenced to customers and regulators who now ask for it.
topics.name: Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)
topics.blurb: Building security into every phase of how software is planned, written, tested and shipped, and what changes when AI writes the code and AI features ship in the product.

topics.body: Governance sets the autonomy an agent is allowed, the actions that require a human, and who owns each agent in the catalog. It decides the risk posture recorded for every agent and makes sure audit evidence, identity, version, approvals, exists for regulators before anyone asks.
topics.name: Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC) Security
topics.blurb: The security risks of building, deploying and running autonomous AI agents: tool and MCP bridges, prompt attacks on dynamic input, agent-made supply chain risk, and failures at machine speed.

program.body: An acceptable use policy for AI only works when it is specific enough to enforce. "Use AI responsibly" is not a rule; "no customer PII in any AI tool that has not been approved through the sanctioning pathway" is. The better programs pair the policy with a way to say yes: a fast-track path for low-risk tools, defined by four tests, whether the tool processes sensitive data, makes autonomous decisions, shares data externally, or keeps persistent memory. A tool that passes all four gets a short security review and provisional approval; one that fails any of them goes to full assessment. When the official channel is quick, people use it, and the shadow shrinks.
program.name: AI Acceptable Use Policies

program.body: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is the one most programs map to, and its four functions line up with a working security program: Govern covers roles and accountability, Map covers the inventory of AI systems and their boundaries, Measure covers testing and the behavioral baseline, and Manage covers runtime controls and remediation. ISO/IEC 42001 adds a certifiable management system, which asks for evidence that controls actually operate rather than that they are documented. The practical point is that a framework is a map of what to prove, not the program itself; the program is the register, the tests and the runtime controls that produce the evidence.
program.name: AI Risk Assessment Frameworks

program.body: AI regulation is arriving through existing law as much as new law. Data protection authorities in Europe read the EU AI Act and the GDPR together, and the FTC acts on AI through consumer protection and privacy rather than an AI statute. The EU AI Act's high-risk obligations, as amended by the Digital Omnibus adopted in July 2026, apply from 2 December 2027 for standalone systems and 2 August 2028 for AI in regulated products; its serious-incident reporting runs on a fifteen-day default clock. The Cyber Resilience Act adds a twenty-four-hour early warning for actively exploited vulnerabilities from 11 September 2026. Inference about individuals in sensitive categories is where enforcement is heading next.
program.name: Regulatory Compliance

program.body: Bias is also a security problem. Poisoned training or fine-tuning data can plant biases and backdoors that pass pre-deployment testing because the triggering conditions never occur during the test, then activate in production. That is why an audit of fairness and behavior cannot be a one-time sign-off. The same discipline applies to how results are judged: deterministic checks, whether a control fired, whether a refusal was logged, whether output matched the required form, are the only verdicts that should gate a release, while a model grading another model is useful for triage and flagging runs a person should read, never the final judge.
program.name: Ethics and Bias Auditing
program.note: Fairness metrics and demographic bias testing are covered only indirectly in Volumes VI to VIII.

program.body: Shadow AI is found by asking, not by prohibiting. Start with one business unit and a structured conversation: what AI tools do your people use, where did they come from, and what data do they touch? The answers are usually more extensive than the security team expects. Everything found goes into the inventory and is tiered on the same four tests used for sanctioning, sensitive data, autonomous decisions, external sharing and persistent memory, then run through the fast track or full assessment. Discovery becomes a quarterly rhythm across every unit, and the sanctioning pathway is what keeps the next round smaller than the last.
program.name: Shadow AI Discovery

program.body: Protecting intellectual property in AI runs in two directions. Inbound, a foundation model provider rarely discloses what its model was trained on, so the questions belong in procurement and contracts: what data trained it, and will ours be used to train it again. Outbound, a model fine-tuned on proprietary data is itself an asset, and query access to it is access to that asset: research going back a decade shows black-box access to a prediction interface can be enough to reconstruct a near-equivalent copy. An AI bill of materials, recording training sources, base model, fine-tuning datasets and libraries, is the record that makes both directions governable.
program.name: Intellectual Property Protection

program.body: Boards can act on a number, not a maturity level. Reporting that the AI program is "at maturity level three" gives a board nothing to fund or hold anyone to; reporting a count of open AI security debt, broken into categories with a burn-down rate per quarter, does. The same rule applies to operating metrics: an autonomous action rate tells the board the security operation has actually changed. And the discipline that makes the report credible is completeness, reporting every metric on the scorecard including the ones that got worse, because the first serious incident will land in whichever metric was left out.
program.name: Board-Level AI Risk Reporting

program.body: The people who know where the AI estate actually is do not work in security. Volume IX makes that the method rather than a complaint: the cloud attack surface map is built in a two day workshop before it is built in a tool, because the inputs are held by the data scientists who know where the notebooks are, the platform engineers who know what the pipelines create, and the finance analyst who can find rented GPU capacity on a card statement. The same workshop is the awareness programme that works. It surfaced three accelerator accounts outside every tool the organisation owned, one holding a full copy of a training dataset on a shared password. None had been set up to evade security; each had been set up to meet a deadline, which is what training has to speak to.
program.name: AI Security Awareness Training
program.note: Awareness as a programme of courses is still not treated; what is treated is the workshop that finds the estate.

program.body: An AI threat model starts from boundaries: the model boundary, where prompt injection enters; the tool boundary, where excessive agency lives; and the output boundary, where improper output handling does damage. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and the Agentic Top 10 supply the defect catalog for each boundary, MITRE ATLAS supplies the technique names, and the AI Vulnerability Scoring System ranks what is found. The threat model must not go stale: model versions and prompts are treated as artifacts whose change requires re-verification, and the threat model generates the test plan that runs as a regression suite before every release.

program.body: Cyber policies were written for unauthorized access, data breach and ransomware, and AI produces losses that fit none of those. An agent that approves fraudulent transactions is not a data breach; an AI-generated compliance answer that turns out wrong is not a cyber incident; an AI decision that leads to a discrimination claim may fall outside the policy entirely. Underwriters have noticed: their questions have moved to AI systems, and a documented control that is not actually operated is the answer that fails. Insurance underwriting is one of the few outside forces with a clock of its own, which makes it a useful check on the security program.
program.name: Cyber Insurance Adjustments
